summary: Defines IPv6 routing requirements for building automation in low-power and lossy networks. It comes from the ROLL working group, which targets routing in industrial, commercial, home and urban settings. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Sensors and switches all over a big building pass messages along like a chain, and this lists what that chain must handle.

questions: how many nodes must a building automation routing protocol support
subtitle: What a routing protocol must deliver for wireless sensors and controllers in commercial buildings.

tldr.problem: Commercial buildings are adding wireless sensors, actuators and controllers, which are constrained devices on lossy links and are installed before any IT network exists.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how building management systems are structured, installed and used, then lists IPv6 routing requirements covering commissioning, scalability, mobility, constrained devices, addressing, manageability, route selection and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document for the ROLL working group. Examples include supporting at least 2,000 nodes and a 120 ms request and response time.

today: RFC 5867 is an Informational document from June 2010, and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It states requirements for ROLL routing in buildings and defines no protocol itself. The home-focused counterpart is RFC 5826.

sections.title: Wireless Building Automation
sections.content:
The Routing Over Low-Power and Lossy (ROLL) networks working group works on routing for low-power and lossy networks (LLNs) in industrial, commercial (building), home and urban settings. This document defines the IPv6 routing requirements for building automation.

Buildings have used pneumatic and then electronic links between sensors and controllers for over one hundred years. Wireless lowers installation costs and lets owners add more sensors for tighter control and energy savings. Applications include HVAC, lighting, physical security, fire and elevator systems. A mix of wired and wireless devices is expected. Actuators and area controllers will be mains-powered, while sensors may be battery-less, battery-powered or mains-powered.

Section 3 and Appendix A are mainly educational. The requirements themselves are in Section 5.
sections.eli5: Big buildings have lots of thermostats, smoke detectors and lights. Making them talk by radio saves wiring, but the radio network has to be planned carefully.

sections.title: How Building Systems Are Built
sections.content:
A building management system (BMS) is a hierarchy of sensors, actuators, controllers and user interface devices, divided into subsystems such as HVAC, fire, security, lighting, shutters and elevators. Sensors sit at the edge and gather data. Actuators change the environment. Area controllers handle a small locale such as a room, and zone controllers cover a larger logical space. Each node can run independently if the higher layers are unavailable.

A BMS is installed outside in: endpoints such as thermostats, lights and smoke detectors go in first and are tested, rooms are joined into subsystems, and only later is the system merged onto the enterprise network. IT networks go the other way, from the inside out. Fire, HVAC and lighting must work before an occupancy permit is issued, so the BMS cannot rely on DHCP, AAA or DNS being available.

The RFC gives typical densities: HVAC room devices about 50 ft. apart with a 3:1 ratio of sensors and actuators to controllers, smoke detectors about every 50 ft., fire pull boxes about every 150 ft., and lighting ballasts about every 10 ft. Security cameras may need up to 1 Mbit/s each, against a few kbit/s for most other sensing.
sections.eli5: Builders put the little devices in each room first and join the rooms together later. So the building's gadgets must be able to work together before the office computer network even exists.

sections.title: Traffic Patterns
sections.content:
Real-time sensor and actuator data mostly stays inside the LLN, while alarms and events travel to higher layers. Each sensor sends about 200 bytes of data to its controller each minute and expects an application acknowledgment. Controllers send at a nominal rate of 6 kbit/minute. Thirty percent of a node's packets go to other nodes in the LLN and seventy percent go to an aggregation device and off the LLN.

Multicast is used at commissioning for discovery, and lighting systems use it to switch banks of lights together. Polled systems have proven not to scale, so most vendors use event-based systems, which are quiet at rest but heavy at startup and during firmware upgrades. A typical quiescent load is 6 kbit/s.

Power failures put heavy stress on the routing algorithms. Most lines-powered devices are ready to access the LLN within 10 seconds of power-up, and routes acquired during startup tend to be oblique because neighbor lists are incomplete. This demands an adaptive routing protocol.
sections.eli5: Most of the time the gadgets whisper small updates. After a power cut they all talk at once, so the network has to cope and then tidy up its routes.

sections.title: Commissioning, Scale, Mobility and Constraints
sections.content:
Commissioning. It MUST be possible to commission devices without an extra tool such as a laptop. Zero-configuration means a node obtains an address and joins by itself. Devices SHOULD route among themselves with no extra infrastructure, and a replacement device must be able to advertise the failed device's old IPv6 address as well as its new one.

Scalability. The protocol MUST support at least 2,000 nodes, of which 1,000 act as routers and 1,000 as hosts. Subnetworks must support up to 255 sensors or actuators, and any device MUST be able to reach any other end to end.

Mobility. Mobile devices in motion should not act as routers. A device moving within one LLN SHOULD re-establish communication within 5 seconds after it stops, and the LLN should converge in under 10 seconds. Moving to another LLN SHOULD take 10 seconds, with convergence in under 20 seconds.

Constrained devices. Non-routing devices SHOULD be implementable in 8-bit devices with no more than 128 KB of memory and routers in 8-bit devices with no more than 256 KB of flash. The RFC's example is a 2,000 mAh battery lasting at least 5 years while sending 200 octets per minute. Last-hop routers MUST buffer messages for sleeping nodes for at least 20 seconds. Routing MUST support anycast, unicast and multicast.

Manageability. The protocol SHOULD have a verbose diagnostic mode and route tracking that reports route quality, hop count and alternate routes.
sections.eli5: Devices should set themselves up and be swappable without a fuss. The network must work with thousands of tiny gadgets, let a wheelchair tracker roam, and be kind to sleepy battery gadgets.

sections.title: Route Selection
sections.content:
The routing protocol MUST support a route quality metric, which SHOULD reflect things like signal strength, available bandwidth, hop count, energy and error rate. Routes MUST be adaptive and converge toward the best value over time. The routing layer SHOULD allow secondary and tertiary routes for use when the primary fails, and SHOULD allow manually configured static preferred routes.

For timing, reactive route discovery SHOULD NOT add more than 120 ms of latency. A request with an expected reply must complete in not more than 120 ms, achievable with 5 or fewer hops in each direction, assuming a quiet network. Routing must support prioritization (QoS routing), so critical traffic such as fire detection is not delayed by less critical traffic.
sections.eli5: The network should pick good paths, keep spare paths, answer quickly, and let an emergency message go ahead of ordinary ones.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Security settings must be configurable on site, and configuring over the network is preferred because devices are numerous and often above ceilings. Policies MUST support dynamic configuration so security can be low during installation and raised network-wide at commissioning. Commercial LLNs should always use encrypted packets, with a key from a trust center, a pre-shared static key, or a well-known default static key.

Authentication SHOULD be optional and fully configurable, should happen on joining or rejoining, and should not be repeated at every hop. Data encryption MUST be supported by all protocol solutions, using a network key and/or an application key. Payload-only encryption avoids re-encrypting at every hop, and the LLN security policy MUST be able to differ from the rest of the facility's IP network. Updates such as dynamic keys must reach sleeping devices when they wake.

The RFC notes that wireless means an attacker may reach the LLN physically even when no wired link leaves the building. It says the operator is free to choose the level of risk against performance, and that this requirements document introduces no new security concerns.
sections.eli5: A school building and a secret lab need different amounts of locking. The network should allow either, and gadgets that nap must still get their new keys.
